title: f83r P2: diagnosis, failure-triggered replacement and ordered aftercare in one case
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED. A complete 84-group paragraph is provisionally modeled as a case description plus a treatment rule. Ordinary treatment may be followed by a specific fallback only on failure; subsequent external treatment has its own order and does not prove the fallback occurred. The owned Celsus architecture supplies a concrete rival to an unconditional recipe or a bath property list.

design.whole_content_draft: Identify the case as acute or prolonged from its signs. Begin treatment with bloodletting and an ordinary measure to move the bowel. If that ordinary measure does not act, use black hellebore as the fallback. Apply external preparations in order, first restraining and later dispersing, ending with the specified preparation. Continue the restricted food/drink regimen; the source also changes water temperature with season. The proposed paragraph is about conditional recommendations, not a transcript in which every mentioned remedy was administered.
coupled_claims: Diagnosis distinguishes acute and chronic presentations rather than equating every symptom to the same state.
Fallback is permitted only by failure of ordinary measures; mentioning the fallback does not establish failure or its execution.
Subsequent treatment has an ordered progression independent of whether the fallback was needed.
design.joint_consequence: Two patients can share diagnosis and final aftercare while differing on whether the replacement remedy is licensed. A successful ordinary response must omit the fallback act but may continue aftercare; a failed response can include it. Reversing the external-treatment stages changes the source instruction even if all remedy names remain present.
concrete_rivals: An unconditional ingredient sequence administers every mentioned remedy and does not preserve the success/failure distinction.
A Balneis property/indication list can state conditions without narrating an intervention-response-dependent replacement.
A complete realized treatment history differs from instructions: a condition can be stated even when its branch is never executed.
lexical_and_syntax_debts: The proposed ordinary/remedy distinctions and response marker are unconfirmed. Multiple earlier mentions of lchedy must remain mentions unless an independently fixed verb binds administration; this is a stated noun/action distinction, not an occurrence-specific rescue.
The positions before and after f83r.14 must jointly determine condition scope. No hidden prior failure is assumed.
dal occurs twice on .14; both retain the same stage meaning and cannot be used once as quantity and once as a connective.
The six whole-word hypotheses do not bind diagnosis, symptoms, external polarity order, seasons or final regimen. Those clauses remain target-alignment debts, not translated content.
Celsus is an owned architectural source, not asserted Voynich provenance. The current task reuses the prior source summary; it does not newly certify a diplomatic full Celsus transcription.
Unlike old P16, no arbitrary warm/cold vector is assigned to qochey or inherited from renderer axes.

additional_evidence.quote: **Primary passage.** Celsus, *De medicina* IV.15.1–4, liver disease. The accessible Latin/English edition is [LacusCurtius, Book IV](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Celsus/4%2A.html), with the Latin locator [De medicina IV.15.1.1](https://latin.packhum.org/loc/836/2/260). Celsus first distinguishes acute from chronic/inveterate cases by signs: right-sided pain and fever/bile/hiccup for the acute picture; hard swollen praecordia, post-meal breathing difficulty, jaw paralysis, then abdominal/leg/foot swelling and wasting for the chronic progression. Treatment starts with bloodletting, then moves the bowel; if ordinary measures do not act, black hellebore is used. External plasters follow a fixed order: first repressing, then hot/dispersing, with iris or wormwood additions, and finally a malagma. The same case then receives hot, sparing food and drink that promote urination; cold things are specifically excluded. The later clause makes a seasonal route distinction for water affusion: hot in winter, tepid in summer.
